justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a broadly stable price trajectory with modest upward drift over time. At the one-day horizon, I anchored close to the prevailing market price, assuming mean-reversion dynamics dominate in the very short run and that no major catalyst was imminent. The slight upward tilt in the one-week and one-month estimates reflects a mild bullish bias consistent with longer-term trend momentum and the general tendency of equity markets to drift higher over moderate horizons when no structural headwinds are clearly visible. The incremental increases are small because I did not have strong conviction about directional acceleration, so the estimates stay close to the anchor price rather than projecting a sharp move.

The confidence interval widths expand predictably as the horizon lengthens, reflecting the compounding of uncertainty over time. At one day, the interval is relatively tight because intraday and overnight price moves in liquid assets tend to be bounded under normal market conditions. By one week, macro data releases, earnings surprises, or shifts in central bank communication can materially move prices, so the band widens. At one month, the uncertainty compounds further as geopolitical developments, sector rotation, and changes in risk appetite become increasingly difficult to anticipate. I also factored in the asset's observed historical volatility as a baseline scaling input for interval width at each horizon.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include unexpected central bank policy shifts — either a surprise rate hike or a pivot signal — which historically produce sharp, outsized moves. A sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data, such as a recession signal or a significant inflation surprise, could drive prices well below my lower bounds. On the upside, a strong earnings beat, a geopolitical resolution reducing risk premiums, or a broad risk-on surge driven by liquidity conditions could push prices above my upper bounds. Tail events like a financial system stress episode or a sudden regulatory shock represent lower-probability but high-magnitude risks that my intervals do not fully capture by construction.

It is worth noting that 90% confidence intervals, by definition, leave a 10% probability mass in the tails, so roughly one in ten outcomes should be expected to fall outside these ranges even under well-calibrated forecasts. My estimates carry model uncertainty on top of market uncertainty, meaning the true coverage of these intervals may be somewhat narrower than intended if volatility regimes shift or if correlations break down in ways not reflected in historical data.
